Agassiz states: <Alternate generation was first observed among the Salpae. These ar8 marine mollusks, without shells, belonging to the family Tunieata. Universality of Anitwalcular Lile.-Living organ- isms are universally diffusedl over every part of the globe. The gentle zephyr wafts from flower to flower invisible, fructifying atoms, which quicken beauty and  fragrance, giving the promise of a golden   fruitage, to gladden and nourish a dependent world: Nature 8 own eweet cunning invests all living things;

The course of Nature is the art of God:"

The microseope  reveals the fact that matter measuring only Tzd&0d of an inch in diameter may be  endowed with vitality, and that countless numbers of animalcules often inhabit a single drop of stagnant water: These monads do not vary in forn, whether in motion or at rest. The life of one, even, is an inex- plicable mystery to the philosopher: Ehrenberg writes: 66 Not only in the polar regions is there a12 uninterrupted development of active  microscopic life, where larger animals cannot exist, but we find that those minute beings collected in the Antaretic expedition of Captain James Ross   exhibit a  remarkable abun- dance of unknown, and often most beautiful forms "

Even the interior of animal bodies is inhabited by animalcules: They have been found in the blood of the frog and the salmon, and in the optic fuid of fishes. Organic beings are found in the interior of the earth, into which the industry of the miner has made extensive excavations, sunk deep shafts, and thus revealed their forms; likewise, the smallest fossil  organisms form subter- ranean strata many fathoms deep: Not only do lakes and inland seas   alound with life, but also, from unknown depths, in vol- canic districts, arise thermal sp1ingx which contain living insects. Were we endowed with & microscopic eye, we might see myriads of ethereal voyagers wafted by on every breeze, as we now be- hold drifting clouds of aqueons vapor: While the continents of carth furnishes evidences of the universality of organic beings, recent observations prove that (( animal life predominates amid the eternal night of the depths of the liquid ocean; "

THE ORIGIN OF LIFE.

The ancients, rude in many of their ideas, referred the origin oflife to divine determination. The thought was crudely ex pressed; but well represented, in the following verse:

66 Then God smites his hands together; And strikes out & soul as a spark; Into the organized glory of things, From the deeps of the dark: "

But every func- tion indicates purpose, every organism evinces intelligent design, and all proclaim a Divine Power: Something cannot come out of nothing: With reason and philosophy, chance is an impossi- bility. Our finiteness is illustratedl hy OM1" initiation into organized being: Emerging from 2 rayless atom, too diminutive for the sight, we gradually develop andl advance to the maturity of those conscious wowers, the exerecise of which furnishes indubitable evidence of OUr' immortality. When   cartilage is   placed upon convex surfaces, the reverse is true. The   Ligaments are white, inelastic, tendinous substances, softer than   cartilage, but harder than membrane. TTheir function is to hind together the bones. The  Synovial Membrane covers the cartilages, and is then reflected upon the ligaments, thus forming a thin, closed sac, called the synovial capsule.

All the synovial membranes secrete & lubricating fuid, termed synovid, which enables the surfaces of the bones and ligaments to move freely upon one another: When this fluid is secreted in excessive quantities, it produces a disease known as 66 dropsy of the joints. 2} There are numerous smaller sacs besides the syno- vial, called bursce aucosce, which in structure are analogous to them, and secrete & similar fluid. Some joints permit motion in every direction;, aS the shonldlers, some in two directions only, as the elbows, while others do not admit of any movement. The bones, ligaments, cartilages, and synovial membrane, are supplied with nerves, arteries, and veins:

When an animal is provide with an internal bony structure, it indicates a high rank in the scale of oganization An elaborate terture of bone is found in H10 class below the vertebrates. Even in the lower order of this sul)-kingdom; which is the highest of animals, bone does not exist, as is the case in some  triles of fishes, such as sharks, ete , and in all elasses below that of the cartilaginous fishes, the intlexible suhstance which sustains the soft parts is either shell 01 some  modification of bone, and is usually found on the outsicle of the body. True  bone, on the contrary, is found in the   interior; and, therefore, in higher animals, the skeleton is always internal, while the soft parts are placed external to the bony frame: While many animals of the lowest   species, being composed of soft gelatinous matter, are buoyant in water; the highest type of animals requires not only & bony skeleton, but also a flexible, muscular system, for locomo- tion in the water or upon the land. Each species of the animal kingdom is thus organically adapted t0 its condition and sphere of  life.
